data.title: Cookie
data.tagline: A cookie is a small piece of data the browser stores by server rules and sends automatically on matching later requests.
data.learningOutcome: You can trace Set-Cookie, browser storage, and the later Cookie request header to inspect a session, and distinguish cookies from Web Storage and backend authentication.
data.description: For example, a login response uses `Set-Cookie` to store a session identifier. When the browser later visits a matching address, it sends a `Cookie` request header so the server can find the session. A cookie is only part of the request round trip, not a complete authentication system, authorization decision, or database; sensitive sessions also need properties such as Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite.

learning.assumes: You have seen a site stay signed in after a refresh and know that browsers can keep some site data.
learning.outcome: You can trace Set-Cookie, browser storage, and the later Cookie request header to inspect a session, and distinguish cookies from Web Storage and backend authentication.

distinctions.label: Browser storage
distinctions.explanation: Cookie is automatically considered for matching HTTP requests; Browser Storage is read by page code and is not automatically sent as a request header.

distinctions.label: Authentication
distinctions.explanation: Cookie can carry a session identifier between browser and server; Authentication is the server-side process of verifying who the requester is.

explanation.title: The response asks the browser to store it
explanation.text: The server sends `Set-Cookie` in a response, and the browser decides whether to store it from its name, scope, and security attributes.

explanation.title: Later requests send it when conditions match
explanation.text: For a matching address, the browser puts sendable cookies in the `Cookie` request header. An HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by page script but can still be sent with a request.

data.boundary: Cookies and localStorage can both keep data in a browser, but cookies enter HTTP requests by rule. A cookie is not a complete authentication system or a database; the server must still verify the session, identity, and permission for each action. Sensitive sessions should use Secure and HttpOnly over HTTPS and choose SameSite for the cross-site need.

lessonPractice.title: The login API returns success, but a refresh makes the user signed out again. What should you inspect first?

options.label: Check whether the response sets a session cookie and the refresh request sends it back
options.feedback: Correct. Follow the set, store, and send steps to learn why the server cannot recognize the session on the next request.

options.label: Write isLoggedIn=true to localStorage so the page keeps showing a signed-in state
options.feedback: A frontend flag changes display only. It does not prove that the server accepts a session or replace a request credential.

options.label: Inspect only the user record in the database, not the browser or request headers
options.feedback: An existing user record does not mean this browser request carries a recognizable session. Check Set-Cookie and the later Cookie header too.

data.agentPrompt: Check whether the login response sets a secure session cookie and whether the protected request after refresh sends it automatically. Do not print the full cookie value; use Network and Storage to verify the session survives refresh, while identity and authorization remain server-side.
